title: Janani Luwum
hookLine: a Ugandan archbishop puts his name to a letter against Idi Amin's killings, and is killed

cards: People are disappearing in Uganda. Neighbors taken at night and never seen again. Fear in the towns.

In Kampala, the capital, the country's Anglican bishops write a letter to the president, Idi Amin. It's polite, and it's terrifying, because it puts in writing what people have been afraid to say aloud.
One of the names on it is the archbishop's. He knows what happens to people who put their names to things like this. He signs anyway.

teach.b: He grew up in northern Uganda, and as a young man he was caught up in the East African Revival, a movement of Christians who met in small groups, confessed their sins to one another out loud, and called each other brother and sister across tribe and class.
That habit of plain speaking stayed with him.

teach.h: HE WENT TO SEE AMIN HIMSELF.
teach.b: As archbishop of the Church of Uganda, he went to see Amin in person to raise the cases of people who had vanished.
After the bishops' letter, he was summoned, accused of plotting, and paraded before soldiers and officials. Then he was taken away. The government announced he had died in a car accident.
The church didn't accept that story, and remembers him as a martyr, killed for what he said.
The Greek word behind martyr is the same word the King James Bible renders witnesses in Acts, where Jesus tells his followers: "ye shall be witnesses unto me."
And in Revelation the same word is used of a man who was killed: "Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you."
A witness, and one who dies for the witness. Luwum is both.

teach.h: FEAR NOT THEM WHICH KILL THE BODY.
teach.b: A line from Jesus speaks to that kind of moment: "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul." It's not a promise that nothing bad will happen.
It's a claim about what fear is allowed to decide. Today his statue stands above the great west door of Westminster Abbey in London, among other modern martyrs. And in Uganda, his day is kept.

how: The Church of Uganda and other Anglican churches commemorate Janani Luwum as a martyr, and in Uganda his day is marked with services, especially in the north where he was born. His statue is among the modern martyrs above the west door of Westminster Abbey.

games.q: you're the archbishop. the bishops have written to the president about the killings. putting your name to it could cost your life. what do you do?
o: leave your name off and let the others sign.
sign it with the other bishops.
keep the letter private and wait.
games.why: Luwum signed. he was summoned, accused of plotting and taken away, and the church remembers him as a martyr.

practice: Bring Uganda to mind, and its neighbors around the great lakes and the long valleys: people getting up for work, children walking to school, a church choir practicing, a market opening.

Then think of anyone there who is afraid tonight, of a government, a gun or a hunger. If you pray, pray for them and for those who still speak up when it's costly; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.
